articles.title: An Ohio man bought a house before marriage and later rented it to his brother; after divorce, an appeals court kept the property his alone and upheld $20,000 in legal fees against his wife
articles.summary: A house purchased before marriage can become a point of dispute during divorce, particularly when a couple has lived in the property and mortgage payments
articles.body: A house purchased before marriage can become a point of dispute during divorce, particularly when a couple has lived in the property and mortgage payments are later made through a joint bank account. In Ohio, a divorce case involving a property bought by a husband six years before his marriage raised questions about whether rental income and financial contributions during the marriage had changed its ownership status. The man had later rented the house to his brother, who continued paying rent while the couple was married.In a November 6, 2026, decision, the Ohio Court of Appeals, First District, upheld the husband's ownership of the property and an order requiring his former wife to pay $20,000 towards his attorney fees. The ruling came in Ellison v. Ellison, case number C-260069, with the judgment available on Justia. The court found that the husband had sufficiently traced the rental income, which exceeded the property's mortgage payments, and that the trial court had properly considered the wife's conduct during the divorce proceedings when awarding legal fees.How the property became part of the divorce disputeStephen Ellison purchased a house on Elbrook Avenue in August 2012, six years before marrying Sherrun Ellison on September 1, 2018. The couple lived there from around September 2017 until August or September 2018, around the time of their marriage.After they moved out, Stephen rented the property to his brother and his brother's wife. According to his testimony, the initial monthly rent was $850, which later increased to $1,000 and eventually $1,500 in 2023. When Sherrun filed for divorce in May 2023, the ownership of the house became one of the unresolved issues. She argued that the property should be treated as marital property because money from their joint bank account had been used to pay its mortgage.She also maintained that the couple had contributed to the property's upkeep during their marriage. Their claimed contributions included replacing the carpet and stove, painting the interior and paying for regular maintenance. However, Stephen disputed these claims. He said the improvements had been completed and paid for before the marriage and that the rental income from his brother covered the mortgage payments.Why the court considered the house his separate propertyDuring the divorce proceedings, Stephen presented a lease agreement with his brother and bank statements showing deposits and transfers that he said came from rental payments. He explained that his brother and sister-in-law paid rent through cash, checks and payment applications. He deposited the money into his personal bank account and then used it to pay the mortgage or transferred it into the couple's joint account to cover the payments.His brother also testified that he and his wife had rented the house since 2017, initially paying $850 a month plus utilities. He confirmed that the rent increased over time and that they eventually paid the full amount, even when payments were sometimes delayed.The trial court accepted their testimony and found that the rental income exceeded the mortgage payments. It also concluded that no marital money or labour had been used for improvements or maintenance that would create a marital interest in the property. The court therefore classified the entire Elbrook property as Stephen's separate property.Why the wife was ordered to pay $20,000 in legal feesThe divorce also involved a separate dispute over attorney fees. Stephen argued that his former wife's actions had increased the cost and duration of the proceedings. His lawyer testified that he had accumulated $56,328 in attorney fees over approximately two years of litigation, excluding trial fees. She described several issues that required additional legal work, including changes in legal representation, withdrawn settlement agreements and disputes involving the children and property.The trial court ordered Sherrun to contribute $20,000 towards those expenses. It considered her conduct during the proceedings and found that some of her actions had unnecessarily prolonged the case. Sherrun challenged the award, arguing that the court had relied on statements made during settlement negotiations and had not properly considered Stephen's own conduct. She also argued that the fee award was punitive.The appeals court rejected these arguments. It explained that Ohio law allows courts to award reasonable attorney fees in divorce cases when doing so is equitable. Judges can consider the parties' financial circumstances and their behaviour during litigation. The court also clarified that a judge does not have to establish serious misconduct before awarding legal fees. A party's conduct can be considered when it unnecessarily increases the time and expense of resolving a divorce.Appeals court upholds the original decisionThe Ohio appeals court found no reason to overturn the lower court's findings. It concluded that the evidence supported Stephen's claim that rental income covered the mortgage and that the house had retained its status as his separate property. It also upheld the $20,000 attorney-fee award, finding that the trial court had appropriately considered the circumstances of the divorce proceedings. The November 6 decision affirmed the original judgment, leaving both the property classification and the attorney-fee order unchanged.The ruling highlights how a property purchased before marriage can retain its separate status when its owner can establish the source of mortgage payments and show that marital contributions did not create an ownership interest. It also demonstrates that courts can consider how spouses conduct themselves during divorce proceedings when deciding whether one should contribute to the other's legal expenses.You use AI every day. articles.summary: A century-old Hollywood Hills estate once associated with a whirlwind celebrity marriage has found a new way to command attention.
articles.body: A century-old Hollywood Hills estate once associated with a whirlwind celebrity marriage has found a new way to command attention. Behind its gated entrance, the sprawling property has witnessed Hollywood parties, celebrity gatherings and a dramatic transformation. Once purchased by pop star Katy Perry and comedian Russell Brand during their brief marriage, the historic residence is now seeking a tenant willing to pay an extraordinary $275,000 every month.A celebrity property with a complicated pastAccording to Realtor, Perry and Brand purchased the three-acre Park Hill Estate, located at 8159 Hollywood Boulevard, for $6.5 million in 2011, approximately a year after getting married. Despite the significant investment, the former couple never moved into the residence permanently.Instead, Perry reportedly used the property as a private wellness retreat, spending time there practising yoga and Pilates. She also occasionally slept in a greenhouse on the grounds, which has since been demolished.Their marriage, however, did not last long enough for the property to become a lasting shared home. Brand filed for divorce towards the end of 2011, with the separation finalised in 2012. The following year, Las Vegas hotelier Lorenzo Doumani acquired the estate for $5.56 million, meaning the former couple sold it at a loss of nearly $1 million.A historic address with Hollywood connectionsThe estate's appeal extends well beyond its association with the former celebrity couple. Built in 1923 by real estate developer C.F. DeWitt, the residence has a history closely connected to the entertainment industry.Music industry pioneer Ralph Peer subsequently owned the property, where his gatherings reportedly attracted legendary performers including Frank Sinatra, Dean Martin and Sammy Davis Jr.Over the years, the estate has continued to draw prominent personalities. According to an exclusive report by he New York Post, celebrities and sporting figures including Drake, Adele, Daniel Kaluuya, Kevin Hart and Formula One champion Lewis Hamilton have spent time at the property. Basketball stars Karl-Anthony Towns and Jimmy Butler have also been among its visitors. Adele reportedly hosted a birthday celebration at the estate.An extensive restoration and an extraordinary rental priceAfter acquiring the property, Doumani undertook an extensive renovation to modernise the century-old residence while retaining its original architectural character. The restoration involved removing the roof and extensively reworking the property, with particular attention given to preserving its historic identity, The New York Post states.The result is a substantially refreshed estate that combines its architectural heritage with the expectations of contemporary luxury living.According to Realtor, the property is currently being marketed at $275,000 per month, having returned to the rental market barely a month after being leased at the same rate. Depending on the season and demand, the monthly asking price can reportedly climb to $395,000.Among Hollywood Hills' most expensive rentalsThe asking price places Park Hill Estate among the most expensive rental properties in the Hollywood Hills, claims the Realtor report. The New York Post reports that the listing is being handled by Serhant broker Patrick Michael and Sarah LaRose Doumani of LA Estate Brokerage, who is married to the property's owner.While another Beverly Hills residence on Lawlen Way reportedly commands $500,000 a month, Park Hill remains an exceptionally expensive proposition within its neighbourhood.From its origins as a 1920s Hollywood residence to its celebrity-filled history and multimillion-dollar restoration, the estate has experienced several transformations. Now, its next chapter depends on finding a tenant prepared to pay a premium for a property where Hollywood history and contemporary luxury meet.Images Courtesy: Facebook and Jack Bremen, Pro Property ShotsReady to Make a Smarter Property Decision? articles.title: In 1943, U.S. Army Air Corps Captain David Fransen mailed his five-year-old daughter a coconut from the Philippines; he carved a smiling face on it and wrote her address on the shell
articles.summary: Discover the touching story of U.S. Army Air Corps Captain David Fransen, who mailed a carved coconut to his daughter during WWII, showcasing the personal connections soldiers maintained with loved ones during wartime. Learn how this unique gesture has become a memorable piece of military history.
articles.body: Between the Second World War and modern times, many military men and women were separated from their loved ones by vast distances. They sent letters and packages back and forth, but sometimes a service member wanted to keep communication simple and personal. US Army Air Corps Captain David Fransen was stationed in the Philippines in 1943. He wanted to tell his five-year-old daughter that he loved her. He carved a coconut with a smile on it, and then sent it through the mail to his daughter, so she would have a keepsake from her father. A coconut became an unusual message from the PhilippinesAccording to Chapman University’s Leatherby Libraries, Captain David Fransen was in the Philippines. He came up with a unique way to communicate with his daughter, Susan. Instead of simply mailing a letter, he sent a coconut. He etched a smiley face on the shell and addressed it with the five-year-old's mailing information, creating the shipping capsule for his palm-sized message.The gesture showed the ingenuity with which servicemen were able to connect with their loved ones through the conflict. Fransen's choice of a coconut made the message especially memorable. It also made the message unique because the coconut could carry both a personal decoration and the information needed for delivery. For a young girl waiting for news of her father, the coconut must have been a memorable reminder.The coconut was among the wartime correspondence later highlighted by the University Centre of American War Letters archive, which collects personal letters and other written records from American servicemen and women, preserving accounts that provide a more intimate understanding of military history. Fransen's coconut stood out because it demonstrated that communication did not always have to take the form of conventional paper letters.Wartime correspondence carried emotional importanceFransen's unusual piece of mail was a part of a larger story of connection between American soldiers abroad and their families. In the Second World War, millions of servicemen and women served overseas and were often separated from loved ones for months or even years. Letters provided one of the main means of sharing information, staying in touch, and reassuring loved ones about family affairs. The amount of mail posed serious problems for the service post office space, with floods of correspondence. The US military devised Victory Mail, or V-Mail, in 1942. It photographed handwritten notes on microfilm for overseas movement, where they were reproduced on smaller sheets of paper.A study in war in history examined how postcards shaped relationships between civilians and military personnel during World War I. Although the study focused on a different form of communication, it highlights how written messages helped maintain connections across great distances. The coconut offered a more unusual way to achieve the same purpose. Rather than sending an ordinary letter or postcard, he chose an object that reflected the environment in which he was serving. The carved, grinning face gave the coconut a personal touch, while the address written on its shell turned it into an unconventional means of communication.A small wartime object became part of historical preservationChapman University's 2015 exhibition drew new attention to his coconut during a celebration of the 70th anniversary of the conclusion of the Second World War. The exhibit, World War 2: The Pacific Theatre, featured letters from American service members who had fought throughout the Pacific. The correspondence was displayed alongside other wartime letters chronicling the experiences of those often broken apart from their loved ones by duty. The archive was formed to collect and maintain correspondence from different times in American military history, providing historians with the type of material that is usually absent from the official record.You use AI every day. articles.title: In 1981, a Cessna with five men aboard radioed ‘we’re losing a hell of a lot’ over Australia’s Barrington Tops and vanished; 45 years later, it remains the only civilian plane lost on the mainland without a trace
articles.summary: On a freezing winter night in August 1981, a small aircraft was battling violent turbulence above a forest in Australia's Barrington Tops.
articles.body: On a freezing winter night in August 1981, a small aircraft was battling violent turbulence above a forest in Australia's Barrington Tops. Inside the cockpit, the pilot was struggling to keep the plane under control as ice accumulated on its wings and crucial flight instruments began failing. Then came a chilling radio transmission: "We're losing a hell of a lot … we're down to six and a half." Moments later, the pilot shouted, "Five thousand!" before the aircraft disappeared from radar. There was no distress beacon, no confirmed crash site and no wreckage. Forty-five years later, the disappearance of the Cessna 210M, registered VH-MDX, remains one of Australia's most baffling aviation mysteries.The aircraft was carrying five men from Queensland to Sydney when it vanished over the rugged Barrington Tops region in New South Wales on August 9, 1981. Despite extensive searches involving police, military personnel, rescue teams and volunteers, neither the plane nor the bodies of its occupants have ever been found. According to the Australian Broadcasting Corporation (ABC), it remains the only civilian aircraft to have crashed on mainland Australia without a trace.A flight that took a terrifying turnThe journey began in Proserpine, in Queensland's Whitsundays, where four passengers had spent a week sailing a yacht north for a friend. They were returning to Sydney aboard the six-seater Cessna, piloted by 52-year-old Michael "Mike" Hutchins. The passengers were Ken Price, 54, Rhett Bosler, 33, Noel Wildash, 40, and Philip Pembroke, 43.The aircraft stopped at Coolangatta to refuel before continuing south towards Bankstown. As it approached the area near Newcastle, Hutchins planned to avoid restricted military airspace around the Williamtown Air Force base by turning inland. That route took the aircraft towards the Barrington Tops, a mountainous region known for its unpredictable weather and difficult flying conditions.At around 7:18 pm, Hutchins reported considerable turbulence and strong downdrafts to air traffic controllers. Within minutes, the aircraft entered cloud. At 7:24 pm, the pilot reported that two important flight instruments, the artificial horizon and the gyroscopically controlled direction indicator, had failed. Another instrument stopped working shortly afterwards.The situation continued to deteriorate. Radar picked up the aircraft at 7:28 pm, showing that it had drifted considerably from its intended route. Hutchins struggled to climb and later reported that ice was accumulating on the aircraft. At 7:34 pm, he said the plane had collected a considerable amount of ice, which was affecting its ability to remain airborne.Less than a minute later, the pilot reported another frightening development: a possible cockpit fire. Although he said the problem appeared to have been resolved, the aircraft was already in serious trouble. At approximately 7:38 pm, Hutchins transmitted the words that would become synonymous with the disappearance: "We're losing a hell of a lot … we're down to six and a half." A flight services officer warned him that the lowest safe altitude in the area was 6,000 feet. Hutchins then called out, "Five thousand!" That was the last recorded transmission. Radar contact was also lost around 7:39 pm.A massive search yielded nothingThe Australian Transport Safety Bureau's predecessor investigated the disappearance and identified severe turbulence, icing and the failure of the aircraft's primary flight instruments as probable contributing factors. The aircraft was not equipped to fly in known or forecast icing conditions, according to the investigation summary. An extensive air and ground search began almost immediately. For nine days, rescue personnel, police, bushwalkers, national parks staff and other volunteers combed the mountainous terrain. Around a dozen aircraft flew over the search area each day, while ground teams navigated slippery rocks, dense vegetation and dangerous gullies.However, the searchers had little certainty about where to look. Their investigation was based largely on the aircraft's final radar positions and conflicting eyewitness accounts. Although several wrecks were discovered during the operation, none belonged to VH-MDX.On August 18, nine days after the disappearance, police suspended the search. They planned to return when weather conditions improved, this time focusing on recovering bodies and wreckage. Subsequent searches also failed to locate the aircraft. The difficult terrain remains a major obstacle. Barrington Tops National Park covers approximately 125,000 hectares and contains ancient rainforests, subalpine woodlands and steep mountain ranges. Thick vegetation can conceal wreckage from aerial searches, while poor visibility and rapidly changing weather make ground operations challenging.Five men, five families and decades without answersBehind the aviation mystery were five families whose lives changed in a matter of minutes. One of the most heartbreaking stories belonged to Philip Pembroke, who had recently become engaged to Yvonne Pembroke. The couple had discovered that they were expecting a child shortly before his trip to Queensland. Yvonne later recalled how Philip had told her before leaving: "Don't you have that baby without me." On the night the aircraft disappeared, she was at a neighbour's house. The neighbour, Gail Bosler, was also waiting for her husband Rhett, who was aboard the plane.Close to midnight, Yvonne received a call informing her that the aircraft had gone down after a fire was reported in the cockpit. The two women, who had been waiting for their partners to return, were suddenly confronted with the possibility that neither man would come home. Philip's eldest son, Andrew Pembroke, was 18 when his father disappeared. He joined the search but soon realised how difficult it would be to locate anything beneath the enormous forest canopy. Speaking to ABC, he described the uncertainty as a form of "slow water torture".The disappearance also sparked numerous conspiracy theories over the years. Some suggested that the men had faked their deaths and escaped overseas, while others alleged drug or gold smuggling, secret military missions and even alien involvement. However, investigations into these claims have found no credible evidence to support them. A coronial inquest held in Sydney in 1982 concluded that the occupants had died when the aircraft crashed in the Barrington Tops area. The coroner also noted that the cause of the accident would probably remain unknown until the wreckage was discovered.The search continues after 45 yearsThe mystery has continued to attract amateur investigators and volunteer search groups. Among those still looking are Glenn Horrocks and Glenn Strkalj, who have spent years studying the disappearance and searching different sections of the mountainous region. Their research and computer modelling have helped establish an outer boundary beyond which they believe the aircraft was unlikely to have travelled. However, the area within that boundary still covers approximately 9,000 square kilometres of dense wilderness.The most recent search by the volunteers took place in June 2026. They are also monitoring newer technologies that could help identify wreckage hidden beneath thick vegetation.For the families, however, the search has never been just about solving an aviation puzzle. Yvonne Pembroke, who raised her son without Philip, told ABC that she still thinks about her fiancé every day. His disappearance, she said, shaped the rest of her life. Even after four and a half decades, the final radio call remains the only recorded glimpse into what happened aboard VH-MDX.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.body: NEW DELHI: The BJP on Monday launched a sharp attack on Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge over his description of Diwali as 'khushiyon ka Eid', with Union minister Giriraj Singh accusing him of practising appeasement politics and attempting to divide Hindus while pandering to Muslims.Reacting to Kharge's remarks, Singh alleged that the Congress president was merely a mouthpiece for Rahul Gandhi and the Gandhi family, accusing him of repeating whatever the party leadership fed him."He is merely a 'loudspeaker'—a mouthpiece—for Rahul Gandhi and the Gandhi family. It only broadcasts whatever is fed into the machine. So, this has been going on for a long time. Kharge-sahab, your true colours have been exposed. You are playing a game of appeasement in this country," Singh said."Nehru divided the nation, and ever since then, you have been practising the politics of appeasement, trying to divide Hindus while pandering to Muslims. You and Rahul Gandhi will never speak up against someone like Irfan Ansari. When a bomb blast occurred in Ghaziabad, aimed at destroying Diwali, you remained silent. You cannot bring yourself to utter even a few kind words regarding our Hindu festivals. This will no longer be tolerated..." he added.Kharge had extended his Diwali greetings over the weekend, describing the festival as 'khushiyon ka Eid' while speaking to reporters. He had said Diwali was a major festival celebrated by everyone in India.The remarks triggered criticism from several BJP leaders, who accused the Congress of compromising the identity of Hindu festivals for political appeasement.BJP spokesperson Gaurav Bhatia questioned why Diwali could not be referred to by its own name, while challenging Kharge and Rahul Gandhi to describe Eid as the 'Diwali of joy'. Another party spokesperson, Tuhin Sinha, also accused the Congress of attempting to associate Hindu festivals with Eid.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: The $500 million gamble to make India’s ‘Ramayana’ a global phenomenon
articles.summary: Can a Hindu epic become the world’s next great movie franchise? Filmmaker Namit Malhotra is about to find out.
articles.body: Namit Malhotra looks awfully relaxed for a man taking a $500 million gamble. Reclining into a sofa in a discreet London office, the movie producer bats away questions about the box office potential and estimated price tag of his two-part blockbuster adaptation of the Hindu epic, “The Ramayana.” “I’m not motivated by the bean-counter logic of, ‘How much money did we make or not make,” he said. “If we don’t make money with the movies, we’ll make it in the merchandise. If we don’t make it in the merchandise, we’ll make it in the theme park. If we don’t make it in the theme park, we’ll make it some other way. “This is the story of Lord Ram, OK? There is no version of this where people don’t like (the movies) and it does not drive economic upside.” “The Ramayana” — or at least this version of it (there are hundreds) — tells the story of Rama, a divine prince who answers the call to defeat Ravana, a demon king whose ambition and power threatened the gods themselves. The source text is a more than 2,000-year-old epic poem, attributed to Hindu sage Valmiki, which recounts a cosmic Manichean battle with a list of heroes longer than “Avengers: Doomsday.” It’s a story that generations of Indians have grown up on, and one that has been adapted many times before, including a beloved 1980s TV serial that ran for over a year. But the epic has never been told on this scale, nor with a global audience in mind. I first met Malhotra in spring, months out from last Thursday’s release of part one, “Ramayana: Rise of a Legend.” He is the CEO of eight-time Oscar-winning British visual effects studio DNEG and founder of Mumbai-based Prime Focus Studios. Talkative and patriotic, Malhotra is a third-generation filmmaker gunning to expand India’s cinematic clout and redefine what audiences think about films from the world’s most populous country. And, unlike most in the movie business, he’s fronting his dream with his own cash. “It’s all my money,” he said. “I have all the risk … I’m going all in.” “Ramayana” is the most expensive Indian film production ever, though an average of $250 million per film puts it in the same ballpark as your typical Marvel movie (or some of the more profligate efforts by streaming giants). However, the most money an Indian film has ever made at the global box office is $304 million — 2016’s “Dangal,” starring Aamir Khan. Factor in “Ramayana’s” globe-hopping marketing campaign and the odds appear stacked against it recouping costs in cinemas. But with the potential wild card of an (as-yet-confirmed) box office release in China — where “Dangal” grossed 64% of its global take — anything is possible. Malhotra has leveraged his little black book to realize this passion project. He hired “Dangal” director Nitesh Tiwari to write and direct both parts. He cast lead actors from across India’s multilingual cinema industries: Hindi star Ranbir Kapoor as Rama, Kannada-speaking actor Yash as Ravana, and Tamil and Teluga star Sai Pallavi as Rama’s wife Sita. He also recruited the cream of Hollywood’s craft departments to bring his vision to life, and half of Bollywood to build it. He asked Hans Zimmer and A.R. Rahman to buddy up on the score and put DNEG — whose credits this year include “The Odyssey” and “Dune: Part Three” — in charge of visual effects. “It should be mounted with the resources and the stars and the director and music like any big Hollywood tentpole,” said Malhotra. “Because until we do that, we will always be the have-nots. We will always feel like we tried and we didn’t get there.” Part one was shot mostly on soundstages in Mumbai. As one might expect for a story featuring a flying palace, demon warriors and a winged elephant, Airavata, the film is an CGI-heavy spectacle. “I’ve never done a movie which had so much visual effects,” said Yash, who also co-produced. The special effect that has made the most headlines is the AI-assisted lip-synced dubbing, from Hindi to English, for the international release. Malhotra said the actors recorded their lines in English and that their voices aren’t AI generated. But a combination of motion capture and AI was used to match mouth and facial movements to the new speech. Overseeing the process was Brahma AI, an Indian tech company valued at $2 billion that is part of DNEG Group. “It’s taken us over a year, and millions of dollars spent” to make the English dub, said Malhotra. Internationally, “Ramayana” is being billed as India’s answer to “Avatar” or “The Lord of the Rings.” One fundamental difference is that it is a religious narrative. “We ourselves are believers,” said Tiwari, speaking of his and Malhotra’s shared Hindu faith. “When you have (the) sensibilities of billions of people attached to an epic, you have to tread very cautiously,” he said. Tiwari explained that the screenplay is based on the two most popular versions of the Ramayana, and included elements from others too. “But everything is from the scriptures,” he clarified. Films inspired by the Ramayana are not guaranteed slam drunks. Just three years ago, big-budget action film “Adipurush” bombed at the box office amid public backlash. Malhotra’s “Ramayana” will face intense scrutiny by India’s cinemagoers, and all eyes are on Kapoor as Rama, an idealized hero broadly worshipped by Hindus. The Bollywood star, first known for romantic comedies, and recently action dramas, said the responsibility was “daunting” and that he was reluctant to take on Rama. “There is a certain professional and personal baggage that I come with,” Kapoor explained. “People have been seeing me on screen for the last 18 years playing different parts.” “I didn’t have confidence in myself,” he admitted. “Will I be able to fit the part? Will I be able to do justice to it? Will the audience accept me? There will always be a conversation, like, ‘He’s not fit to play this part.’” Kapoor said “sense prevailed” and he signed on. “I don’t think I will ever, ever get (another) opportunity like this to tell a story like this. It’s not about the money spent, or the fact that it was going to be a global film. It’s just being a part of a story which we worship. Our value systems, our moral codes have been derived from these stories.” “Ramayana” arrives amid a recent wave of big-screen adaptations of ancient epics and mythology. Christopher Nolan’s “The Odyssey,” based on Homer’s epic, drew audiences to theaters this summer, while Chinese animation “Ne Zha 2,” inspired by Chinese mythology, became the world’s highest-grossing movie of 2025. The latter grossed $2.2 billion in China alone, aided by a Lunar New Year release and reports that companies booked screenings for employees and subsidized tickets. Part one of “Ramayana” was released just days before Diwali, which is associated with Rama’s return home from exile. The filmmakers will have been hoping to seize on the celebratory mood, and are pitching the movie to the whole nation, not just the Hindi-speaking population. Some of the creative decisions have been calculated to broaden appeal. “Ramayana is every Indian’s story,” said Malhotra, explaining why he cast actors from across the country. “What was very important was for us to really make it feel like (the film is) from India first; that it’s not from Bollywood.” Joyojeet Pal, professor of information at the University of Michigan, saw sense in touting the movie as an industry unifier. “It is important to do that, because a lot of the discourse around the spate of nationalistic films out right now is that they present a sectarian view of India that tends to be dominated by a North Indian, Hindu-oriented narrative,” he explained. “There is another, more complicated side to the narrative in that the main antagonist of the dominant version of ‘The Ramayana,’ Ravana, is seen as a heroic character in parts of the south,” Pal added. “Thus, presenting a pan-Indian narrative is valuable as part of its branding.” Yash predicted lively scenes in Indian movie theaters come opening weekend. “I think it’ll turn into a stadium there, or like a music concert,” he said. “There is a collective experience that (Indian audiences) all want to feel at the cinemas,” added Kapoor. “They root for you; at the same time, when you disappoint them, they will also criticize you. And we love that. We love the fact that they have the ability to do both. The power is in the audience’s hands. “It’s a dream job to be an actor in Indian cinema, and we hope that we can continue being actors and continue to be accepted there,” he said. How “Ramayana: Rise of a Legend” will be received abroad, and if it can surpass diaspora appeal, will be its biggest test. “In India we love world cinema,” said Pallavi. “So, it’ll be nice if it’s (the other way) around.” The film grossed more than $55 million globally on its opening weekend, including $12.2 million in the US, according to Deadline. While it now appears unlikely that “Ramayana” will beat Hindi record-breaker “Dhurandhar: The Revenge,” which grossed $115.3 million worldwide in its first week March, it is nonetheless on course to join India’s highest grossing movies of all time. Back in Malhotra’s office earlier this year, the producer had been buoyant. “I don’t want to sound spiritual as a businessman,” he said. “But honestly … you can’t do this right and not succeed.” “To me, there’s one fundamental truth: that if we do ‘Ramayana’ well, and if people like it, financially we’ll be fine,” he added. “That’s my fundamental belief. There’s no way to argue it. There’s no way to debate it. And I don’t think anybody in the world is smart enough to counter it with scientific or commercial logic.”

articles.title: 12 migrants found dead in boat off Greece's Crete as hundreds arrive from Libya
articles.summary: Greek authorities recovered 12 bodies from a boat carrying migrants off the southern coast of Crete on Monday, while a passing cargo ship rescued 18
articles.body: Greek authorities recovered 12 bodies from a boat carrying migrants off the southern coast of Crete on Monday, while a passing cargo ship rescued 18 survivors from the same vessel, the coast guard said.The boat was located about 15 nautical miles (28 km) south of Crete early on Monday. Authorities have not yet disclosed the identities of those who died or the circumstances surrounding their deaths.Two other boats carrying 47 and 40 people were also spotted sailing south of the island. All the rescued migrants were being taken to a port on Crete's southern coast, the Associated Press reported.The incident comes amid a sharp increase in migrant arrivals on the island from Libya, prompting Greece to prepare for a possible migration crisis.Greece prepares for migration crisis on CreteMigration and asylum minister Thanos Plevris said 1,700 people had arrived from Libya in the first three days of November. He attributed the increase to a breakdown in cooperation with Libyan authorities and linked it to the Turkey-Libya maritime memorandum, according to eKathimerini."We are preparing for a crisis on Crete," Plevris said. A reception facility at Athanati is expected to open next week.The increase in arrivals on Crete comes despite a broader decline in irregular migration to Greece and across the European Union, according to the European Commission's second annual report, presented on Thursday.Between July 2025 and June 2026, irregular crossings into Greece fell 23 per cent, while asylum applications declined 19 per cent. However, Greece continued to face the EU's highest proportional pressure on both measures when assessed against population and gross domestic product.Arrivals on Crete increased 105 per cent to around 21,000, while crossings along Greece's land border with Turkey rose 33 per cent. Across the Eastern Mediterranean route, irregular crossings fell about 25 per cent to 49,136. The EU-wide figure declined 32 per cent to 151,877, eKathimerini reported.Greece accounted for 25 per cent of disembarkations following search-and-rescue operations across the bloc, compared with 42 per cent for Italy. A European official said Greece continued to face disproportionate pressure and qualified for EU assistance in 2027.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: At 17, Florida student Megan Markus founded a letter-writing project for incarcerated people; in 18 months, volunteers have sent more than 5,200 letters across all 50 US states and 105 countries and territories
articles.summary: A simple letter can offer something that people behind prison walls may go without for years: a reminder that they are not forgotten.
articles.body: A simple letter can offer something that people behind prison walls may go without for years: a reminder that they are not forgotten. In Florida, 17-year-old high school student Megan Markus has turned this idea into a global volunteer initiative, sending messages of hope and human connection to incarcerated people. Through her youth-led organisation, Paper Wings Project, she and a network of volunteers have sent more than 5,200 letters across all 50 US states and 105 countries and territories in just 18 months.Points of Light featured Markus in its Daily Point of Light series on November 5, 2026, recognising her efforts to connect with people in prisons through handwritten correspondence. The initiative also encourages recipients to write back, creating opportunities for personal conversations rather than one-way exchanges. What began as a way to combine her passion for writing with her interest in criminal justice has also led to a second initiative, Chrysalis Review, a literary and arts magazine that gives incarcerated writers and artists an opportunity to share their work.What inspired Megan to start Paper Wings Project?Growing up in Pinecrest, Florida, Markus was exposed to discussions about the criminal justice system through her parents, both of whom are criminal defence lawyers. These conversations made her aware of the challenges within the US justice system and its emphasis on punishment rather than rehabilitation. Writing had always been an important part of her life. She began looking for a way to connect her interest in language with her desire to support people affected by incarceration.About a year and a half ago, she established Paper Wings Project, a youth-led nonprofit that sends letters to people serving time in prisons. Her aim was to remind recipients that their voices and experiences matter, regardless of their circumstances. Markus believes that people should not be defined entirely by their criminal records. While she acknowledges that individuals must be held accountable for their actions, she also believes they deserve dignity, human connection and opportunities for personal expression.How the letter-writing initiative worksPaper Wings Project relies on volunteers who help write letters and respond to messages received from incarcerated individuals. For its work in the United States, the organisation searches state and federal prison databases to identify people who can receive correspondence. The first letter also encourages recipients to spread the word among other people in their facilities so that more individuals can participate.International outreach requires a different approach because many countries do not maintain publicly accessible databases of incarcerated people. In such cases, the organisation contacts prison officials directly and asks them to share information about the project and its invitation to contribute writing and artwork to Chrysalis Review. An important part of the initiative is its commitment to responding to everyone who writes back. Volunteers prepare personal replies, allowing recipients to become active participants in the correspondence.According to Markus, the responses have been among the most meaningful parts of the project. She recalled receiving a letter from someone who had not exchanged personal correspondence in 27 years. Others have shared how receiving a message made them feel valued and remembered.Chrysalis Review gives incarcerated artists a platformThe success of Paper Wings Project inspired Markus to establish a second initiative called Chrysalis Review. It is a biannual literary and arts magazine dedicated to publishing creative work by incarcerated writers and artists. The publication gives people in prisons an opportunity to share their experiences, ideas, writing and artwork with a wider audience.Its first issue, titled Cocooned, was published in March 2026. The theme explored the difficult and often uncomfortable process of transformation, drawing inspiration from the dark, confined environment inside a butterfly's chrysalis. The organisation is working on its second issue, titled Breaking Free, which is expected to focus on reintegration and the challenges people face when returning to society.For Markus, the magazine is another way to ensure that incarcerated individuals have opportunities to express themselves rather than being defined only by their past actions.Why she believes human connection mattersMarkus has also faced questions about whether giving incarcerated people a platform means overlooking their crimes. Her response is that the project's purpose is not to judge their circumstances or excuse wrongdoing. Instead, she wants to recognise their humanity and provide space for personal expression. She believes that accountability and human dignity can exist together.The experience has also changed how she views volunteering. She describes it as a two-way relationship rather than an arrangement in which one person gives and another simply receives. The letters have affected the volunteers as much as they have helped recipients. Markus recalled reading some of the first responses with her father, an experience that moved both of them to tears.Through more than 5,200 letters and a growing creative platform, the teenager's initiative has created opportunities for people behind bars to communicate, share their stories and feel connected to the outside world. For Markus, every letter is a reminder that meaningful human connection can begin with a small act of kindness.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: India's Prachand, Apache fleet vs Pakistan's 30 Chinese Z-10ME helicopters: How they compare
articles.summary: Pakistan's reported procurement of 30 Chinese-made Z-10ME attack helicopters has brought renewed attention to the modernisation of its Army Aviation
articles.body: Pakistan's reported procurement of 30 Chinese-made Z-10ME attack helicopters has brought renewed attention to the modernisation of its Army Aviation Corps, which has been looking to replace its ageing American-built Bell AH-1F Cobra fleet. The reported contract, details of which emerged through an image circulated on Chinese media, would mark a major addition to Pakistan's attack helicopter inventory. However, neither Islamabad nor Beijing has officially confirmed the reported order or the number of helicopters involved. The report comes as India expands its own fleet of Light Combat Helicopters (LCH) Prachand, built for mountain warfare.The report comes from an image on Chinese social media, shared by a military blogger known as Sashoujian. It claims that China National Aero-Technology Import and Export Corporation (CATIC) signed a contract with Pakistan's defence ministry for 30 Z-10ME helicopters, with associated equipment and services. The image does not give the year and has not been independently verified, and neither Islamabad nor Beijing has confirmed the order. Pakistan did formally induct the helicopter on August 2, 2025, at Multan Garrison, in a ceremony led by Army chief Field Marshal Asim Munir, though it did not disclose how many were inducted.The Z-10ME is an export variant of China's Z-10, built by Changhe Aircraft Industries Corporation (CAIC). It carries extra armour, missile approach warning sensors, radar warning systems, countermeasures and a millimetre-wave radar above the main rotor. Its armament includes anti-tank guided missiles, air-to-air missiles, rocket pods and a cannon.Why Pakistan turned to ChinaThe Army Aviation Corps has been trying to replace its ageing American-built Bell AH-1F Cobra helicopters since 1985. In April 2015, the US State Department approved a possible sale of 15 AH-1Z Viper helicopters worth an estimated $952 million, but the planned deliveries did not take place after Washington froze military aid to Pakistan in 2018. Islamabad then signed a $1.5 billion contract in 2018 with Turkey for 30 T129 ATAK helicopters. That deal stalled because the US withheld export licences for the engines made by the Light Helicopter Turbine Engine Company (LHTEC), and Pakistan eventually abandoned it and turned to the Z-10.India's high-altitude answerIndia's Prachand is designed for mountain operations and, according to the Ministry of Defence (MoD), can take off and land at 5,000 metres with adequate fuel and payload. The Indian Air Force (IAF) inducted its first helicopters in October 2022 as part of 15 limited-series production helicopters, 10 for the IAF and five for the Army. On March 28, 2025, the MoD signed two contracts worth Rs 62,700 crore with Hindustan Aeronautics Limited (HAL) for 156 helicopters, 90 for the Army and 66 for the IAF. Deliveries are due to begin in the third year of the contract and run over the next five years, with more than 65% indigenous content and over 250 domestic firms involved.The Prachand carries a 20mm turret gun, 70mm rocket pods and air-to-air missiles, and is powered by two Shakti turboshaft engines, with a service ceiling of 6,500 metres. The weaponised version of the ALH Dhruv, the Rudra is the most numerous armed helicopter in the country, this chopper in service with both the army and IAF. The Rudra is equipped to carry a 20mm cannon and 70mm rockets. This helicopter, along with the Prachand, will get the Helina and the Dhruvastra missile soon.The Indian attack helicopter fleet also consists of 28 Boeing AH-64E Apache, which functions as the heavy, network-centric element. It is armed with AGM-114 Hellfire missiles and Longbow radar. The IAF operates 22 of these advanced choppers, while the army operates the remaining six. India also operates the Russian-origin Mil Mi-35 attack helicopters, which will be retired from service in the coming years.How India and Pakistan's attack choppers comparePlacing the two helicopters side by side shows how differently they were designed. The Z-10ME is a medium-weight platform with a maximum take-off weight of around 7,000-7,200 kg, powered by two WZ-9G engines that reportedly produce about 1,500 shaft horsepower each. Its top speed is around 300 kmph, and its range is reported at about 800 km, though published figures vary. The Prachand is lighter, at 5,800 kg, with two Shakti engines, developed by HAL with Safran, of about 1,400 shaft horsepower each. It has a cruise speed of 270 kmph, a range of 580 km and an endurance of around four hours.The biggest difference is the ability to operate at the higher altitudes of the Himalayas. The Prachand has a service ceiling of 6,500 metres and can take off and land at 5,000 metres with adequate fuel and payload, which matters in eastern Ladakh, Siachen and other high areas along both the Line of Actual Control as well as the Line of Control. The Z-10ME has had engine and airframe upgrades, but public information does not show an equivalent demonstrated capability with a substantial combat load. A service ceiling should not be confused with the ability to operate from high-altitude helipads carrying weapons and fuel.The Z-10ME carries a 23mm cannon and has four external weapon stations, with missiles reportedly drawn from China's KD-9, KD-10 and HJ-10 families, which gives it a more extensively documented anti-armour package. The Prachand has a 20mm turret gun, 70mm rocket pods and air-to-air missiles, with the indigenous Dhruvastra anti-tank missile being integrated. The Z-10ME's millimetre-wave radar above its rotor lets it scan for targets from behind ridgelines, and HAL lists no comparable radar for the Prachand.The Prachand has the advantage in publicly demonstrated high-altitude performance, and the Z-10ME in a better-documented radar and anti-armour fit. A definitive comparison of combat effectiveness is hard to make, because independently verified data on the Chinese helicopter, particularly its high-altitude payload and sensors, is not available.

articles.title: Delhi pollution sparks row: BJP alleges 'conspiracy'; AAP and Congress question AQI data
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: A thick blanket of smog engulfed Delhi on Monday, with air quality deteriorating to the brink of the 'severe' category a day after Diwali
articles.body: NEW DELHI: A thick blanket of smog engulfed Delhi on Monday, with air quality deteriorating to the brink of the 'severe' category a day after Diwali celebrations. As several monitoring stations recorded an Air Quality Index (AQI) above 400, a political war of words erupted between the BJP, Aam Aadmi Party (AAP) and Congress.Delhi minister Kapil Mishra accused the AAP government in Punjab of orchestrating stubble-burning incidents on Diwali to deliberately worsen Delhi's air quality and target the festival. Congress leader Pawan Khera questioned the Delhi government's pollution data, alleging that readings from several monitoring stations had gone missing during the night.Kapil Mishra alleges conspiracy over Punjab farm firesDelhi minister and BJP leader Kapil Mishra alleged that a sudden increase in stubble-burning incidents in Punjab on Diwali was a premeditated attempt to worsen pollution in the national capital. He demanded an investigation by Punjab chief minister Bhagwant Mann and called for FIRs against those responsible.Speaking about the allegations, Mishra said he and BJP leader Sirsa had started receiving calls from farmers in Punjab reporting that their fields were being set on fire while they were celebrating Diwali at home.He said the claims initially appeared difficult to believe, prompting them to examine satellite data on stubble burning made available to the Government of India."We decided to find out the truth...We asked for data coming in through satellites for Govt of India on stubble burning. The data proves that this was a premeditated move, and fields in Punjab were set on fire," Mishra said.Citing the figures, he claimed that stubble burning was recorded at 125 locations on November 7, but the number jumped to 1,200 on November 8, coinciding with Diwali."How did it increase 10 times?...This is a really serious matter. This is a conspiracy against farmers, against Diwali, against Delhi, against Punjab," he said.Mishra also urged the Punjab chief minister to investigate the alleged fires and examine the phone records of AAP members from Delhi who were in Punjab, claiming that a campaign had been launched two days before the festival to blame the BJP government for rising pollution.Pawan Khera questions missing pollution dataCongress leader Pawan Khera took aim at the BJP government over the deteriorating air quality, alleging that pollution readings from several monitoring stations in Delhi were unavailable during the early hours of November 9.In a sharp attack, Khera congratulated Delhi for getting a "double-, triple- or whatever-engine Sarkaar", accusing the government of moving stealthily while allowing the city's residents to choke."There were no PM2.5 readings recorded at 25 of Delhi’s 39 monitoring stations between 2 and 3 a.m. on the night of November 8–9. WHY?" he asked.Khera questioned whether the government was suppressing pollution data, whether monitoring equipment had been deliberately switched off or whether pollution levels had exceeded the equipment's measuring capacity."Whatever the reason, the government owes the people of Delhi an explanation," he said.He further alleged that the absence of readings did not mean pollution had disappeared, warning that the toxic air continued to threaten people's health and life expectancy. He also accused the BJP of failing to acknowledge the severity of the crisis. Praveen Khandelwal blames previous governmentsBJP MP Praveen Khandelwal also accused the AAP of deliberately allowing stubble burning in Punjab to worsen Delhi's pollution during Diwali."This is a well-thought-out conspiracy. Aam Aadmi Party has a government in Punjab, and the people of Punjab are crying for help. Punjab decided to burn stubble vigorously so that Delhi remains polluted on Diwali and they can blame us for it," he said.Khandelwal also blamed successive Congress and AAP governments for failing to address the pollution problem, arguing that the BJP government would need time to reverse years of inaction.AAP alleges manipulation of AQI readingsAAP Delhi unit president Saurabh Bhardwaj, meanwhile, accused the BJP government of manipulating pollution figures to present a better picture of Delhi's air quality.He alleged that monitoring stations had been shut down and that 20 new AQI stations had been installed in remote, green areas of the capital. He also claimed that water was being sprinkled directly over monitoring stations in polluted areas to influence readings."The government's data is based on fraud. We showed how monitoring stations were shut down, and how 20 new AQI stations were installed in remote, lush green areas of Delhi. Water is being sprinkled directly over the monitoring stations in polluted spots to manipulate the readings. People simply do not trust the government's AQI numbers; I certainly don't," Bhardwaj said.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Russell Brand faces sentencing after conviction for raping, sexually assaulting four women
articles.summary: British comedian and actor Russell Brand faces sentencing on Monday after being convicted of sexually abusing four women, bringing renewed scrutiny to
articles.body: British comedian and actor Russell Brand faces sentencing on Monday after being convicted of sexually abusing four women, bringing renewed scrutiny to allegations that emerged alongside his once-publicly celebrated image of sexual exploits and promiscuity.Brand, 51, could face a substantial prison sentence after a jury found him guilty of raping one woman and sexually assaulting three others. Throughout the proceedings, he maintained his innocence, insisting that all his sexual encounters had been consensual.However, the jury, comprising eight men and four women, rejected his defence and convicted him on four of the seven charges relating to allegations dating back to 2004. He was acquitted of two counts of rape and one count of attempted indecent assault.His own statements about his sexual behaviour and widely documented history of promiscuity also featured prominently during the trial, according to news agency AP.Prosecutor Riel Karmy-Jones described Brand as a ruthless, calculating and manipulative 'sexual predator', accusing him of treating women as 'disposable commodities'.To highlight his attitude towards relationships and sexual encounters, she referred to passages from his 2007 memoir, 'My Booky Wook'. In the book, Brand wrote: 'If I want something — whether it's a job or a woman — I will determinedly, resolutely, remove anything that's in the way, until I possess the object of my desire.'The allegations against Brand gained widespread attention following a 2023 investigation by The Times and Channel 4. The investigation featured accounts from women who accused the comedian of sexually abusing and degrading them.The four convictions relate to separate incidents involving different women. Brand was found guilty of sexually assaulting a woman during a birthday celebration at a London bar in 2004. However, he was acquitted of the charge of orally raping her in a restroom.He was also convicted of kissing and groping another woman at a London radio station in 2004 or 2005. Another conviction involved the rape of a fan at his home in 2009, after she had met him backstage following one of his comedy performances.The fourth conviction concerned an incident during the recording of an advertisement in 2009. The woman alleged that Brand demanded a massage and pushed his face into her groin.Brand was acquitted of raping another woman in a hotel room during the labour party's annual conference in Bournemouth in 1999. He was also cleared of attempting to indecently assault a woman by allegedly dragging her towards the men's bathroom at the London offices of music channel MTV.The associated press does not identify victims of alleged sexual violence. British law also guarantees lifelong anonymity to complainants in such cases.Brand rose to prominence in the early 2000s through his provocative stand-up performances, television appearances and a BBC radio show. Known for his struggles with drug and alcohol addiction, he subsequently established himself in Hollywood, appearing in films such as 'Forgetting Sarah Marshall' and 'Get Him to the Greek'. He was also briefly married to pop star Katy Perry.In recent years, Brand has distanced himself from mainstream entertainment and moved to Florida, where he has developed a substantial online following. His digital content features discussions on wellness, conspiracy theories and his growing interest in religious faith.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: North Dakota parents gave a son an option to buy farmland for $100 an acre if he returned and farmed; after an inheritance fight, the Supreme Court ruled he failed the condition and ordered rent damages reconsidered
articles.summary: A North Dakota man has lost his claim to buy his parents' farmland for $100 an acre after the state Supreme Court ruled that he failed to meet a condition
articles.body: A North Dakota man has lost his claim to buy his parents' farmland for $100 an acre after the state Supreme Court ruled that he failed to meet a condition set out in their wills. The parents had offered their son, Todd Stramer, the option to purchase the remaining farmland at the fixed price if he returned to North Dakota and actively farmed it. According to the ruling dated Friday, the court upheld the finding that Todd had not fulfilled this condition. It also ordered a lower court to reconsider damages for his use of the farmland between 2023 and 2025.The dispute began after William and Elaine Stramer made their wills in July 2013. The couple had five children, Todd, Ann, Douglas, Steve and Matthew. Their wills gave Todd the option to buy the remaining farmland for $100 an acre. However, he had to move back to North Dakota and actively farm the property. He also had to exercise the option within one year of the death of the surviving parent.According to the offer, if Todd completed the purchase, he would also receive the farm machinery, equipment and the balance in the checking account. William died in January 2015, and Todd moved back to North Dakota. Elaine died in November 2022. Todd then informed the estate that he wanted to exercise his purchase option.However, his siblings challenged his claim. The dispute eventually reached the North Dakota Supreme Court, which examined whether Todd had actually been farming the property as required by his parents.Why the court rejected his claimFor the 2023 farming season, Todd arranged for Mike Appert, a longtime tenant of the family, to grow corn and soybeans on the land. Appert supplied the seeds and used his own employees and equipment to plant, spray and harvest the crops.Todd did not pay rent for the farmland. The Elaine Stramer Irrevocable Trust paid the farming expenses and reported the profits and losses in its tax filings.Todd argued that he had taken an active role in managing the farming operation. The lower court accepted that he had contributed to its management. However, it found that he had not independently provided enough money, equipment or land for the operation.The court examined the federal Farm Service Agency's definition of being actively engaged in farming. Under this definition, a person must contribute capital, equipment or land, along with personal labour or management. The person's share of profits or losses must also match their contribution, and they must face a financial risk.The Supreme Court agreed with the lower court's use of this definition. The couple's estate planning lawyer, Charles Chapman, told the trial court that William Stramer had used the expression while referring to federal farm programmes.Chapman recalled asking William what active farming meant. William replied that "anybody who knows anything about farming knows what that means".The court also considered testimony from Appert, who had been farming for more than 35 years and worked on about 47,000 acres.The records showed that the family trust paid for the farming operation. Todd did not use his own money to fund it or maintain a separate business account. Appert provided the equipment, while the trust paid for its use.The Supreme Court said Todd could have contributed by leasing the land or equipment at fair market value. However, he did not do so. His interest in the farmland through the purchase option was not enough to meet the requirement.The court therefore upheld the finding that Todd had not actively farmed the property within the required period. He could not validly exercise the option to buy it.Sister seeks compensation for use of farmlandThe case also involved Todd's role in managing his mother's estate and trust. After Elaine's death, he became the personal representative of her estate and was named trustee of the Elaine Stramer Irrevocable Trust.His sister Ann sought his removal from both positions in 2023. The lower court removed him after finding that he had violated his duties. The Supreme Court upheld this decision.Ann also challenged the lower court's refusal to award compensation for Todd's use of the farmland between 2023 and 2025.She argued that he should pay $700,104 for the three years. Her calculation was based on the $233,368 rent that Appert had paid for the farmland in 2022.The Supreme Court agreed that Todd's occupation of the property was wrongful because he had failed to meet the condition for buying it. It said the estate was entitled to damages for the use of the land.However, the court said the full rent from the property could not be used to calculate the amount owed to Elaine's estate. The farmland was divided into two equal interests. One half belonged to the William Stramer Disclaimer Trust, while the other half belonged to Elaine's estate.Appert had paid $233,368 in rent for 2,333.68 acres in 2022. The amount was divided into two equal payments of $116,684, one for each trust. The Supreme Court said the rental value of Elaine's half was therefore $116,684 a year.The court said compensation could be calculated using either the fair rental value of Elaine's share or the income generated from it. However, the records did not clearly establish who received all the farming income between 2023 and 2025.It reversed the lower court's decision on damages and sent the matter back for the amount to be calculated.Court also limits brother's claim to landThe Supreme Court also considered a separate claim by Todd's brother Douglas, who wanted to buy land around his house.Their parents' wills gave Douglas an option to purchase the immediate farmyard for $100 an acre. He argued that this covered 25 acres identified in a survey completed in November 2014.However, the court found that the survey had been prepared for a proposed purchase that included additional land for Douglas's beekeeping business. It was not meant to identify the farmyard covered by the will.Douglas had testified that the actual farmyard measured about 5.96 acres. The Supreme Court ruled that his purchase option covered 5.96 acres, not the entire 25 acres.The court partly upheld and partly reversed the lower court's decisions. It sent the case back for the judgment to be amended and for damages arising from Todd's use of the farmland to be calculated.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Less controversial, more ‘extraOrdinary’
articles.summary: Explore The Metropolitan Museum of Art's upcoming exhibition, 'extraORDINARY: Fashion and the Poetics of the Everyday,' featuring how simple garments are transformed into extraordinary fashion statements.
articles.body: Two months after The Metropolitan Museum of Art and John Galliano jointly announced in August that the planned exhibition dedicated to the designer would not go ahead, anticipation had been building around what would replace it. The wait ended last week, when The Met unveiled its Spring 2027 Costume Institute exhibition, titled “extraORDINARY: Fashion and the Poetics of the Everyday”. Moving away from the couture grandeur of the Met Gala, the new theme turns the spotlight on the beauty of the everyday, exploring how designers transform familiar garments such as jeans, T-shirts and puffer coats into extraordinary creations. Basically (pun intended), you could walk into an exhibition of this stature wearing nothing more than a simple white T-shirt and jeans, and fit right in!BACKGROUNDThe Costume Institute’s original plan for 2027 was to stage a retrospective of John Galliano’s work. However, the proposal faced opposition from donors, politicians and Jewish leaders in New York City. The criticism centred on Galliano’s 2011 conviction in France over antisemitic and racist remarks. Some donors reportedly approached Met executives and threatened to withdraw their financial support if the retrospective went ahead.Following the backlash, Galliano issued a statement that read, “After much reflection and discussion with all those involved, I have decided, with great sadness, that it is best for the exhibition not to take place at this time...”The Metropolitan Museum of Art has announced its Spring 2027 Costume Institute exhibition, extraORDINARY: Fashion and the Poetics of the Everyday, exploring how everyday garments and objects can be reimagined as high fashion. Think blue denim, white T-shirts and puffer jackets, alongside paper, plastic, metal and bubblewrap, transformed into new creations.TOO ORDINARY, NOT REALLY!The Costume Institute offered a glimpse of the theme through archival looks shared on Instagram, including a deconstructed sweatsuit with a dramatic gold train from Jun Takahashi’s Undercover Fall/Winter 2024-25 collection; layered flannel plaids, striped slip dresses and combat boots from Marc Jacobs’ Perry Ellis Spring 1993 ‘Grunge’ collection; and a tan trench coat draped backwards to frame a metal breastplate from Jonathan Anderson’s Loewe Spring/Summer 2022 collection. These are among the historical looks expected to feature in the exhibition. The looks highlight how designers have turned everyday clothing and familiar objects into works of art. Exploring the extraordinary possibilities of the mundane, the exhibition will open on May 9, 2027, following the Met Gala on the preceding Monday.A nod to Chanel’s Métiers d’Art subway show, Bhavitha Mandava’s Met Gala look was designed by Matthieu Blazy. What appeared to be a casual denim-and-sweater ensemble was, in fact, an intricately hand-crafted trompe l’œil creation.Actress Cate Blanchett's 2024 red-carpet look by Swedish sustainable label Hodakova offers an example of how everyday objects can be elevated into high fashion. Her halter top and suit, embellished with antique silver spoons, resonate with the Met's Spring 2027 theme of finding the extraordinary in the ordinary.JEANS & T-SHIRTS COULD BE THE STARS OF MET GALA 2027Andrew Bolton, the Costume Institute’s curator in charge, said he hopes visitors will attend the exhibition wearing their own versions of jeans, T-shirts and jackets. “I want visitors to leave looking differently at the clothes they arrived in... With a greater sense of what is worth noticing, valuing and caring for,” he said. That said, the gala’s dress code is still under wraps, although Bolton’s statement could hint at a dress code inspired by the exhibition’s theme. According to The New York Times, the exhibition will feature 200 to 230 pieces, around 30 to 40 per cent of which will come from the museum’s own collection, with the rest donated or loaned by fashion houses.The cancellation of the Galliano show was disappointing for everyone involved... I committed myself to this (theme) really quickly because it brings up ideas of value and consumption and resourcefulnessTHE INTERNET HAS ITS SAYWhile some netizens have called the theme boring, others see it as a sign of a recession. Some have questioned why the museum did not instead honour another major fashion name the world has recently lost. While critics and fashion commentators are curious to see how everyday clothing will be reimagined, they are also questioning whether the theme is a creative choice or an attempt at reputation management, with some suggesting the Met is playing it safe following the backlash over its original plans.You use AI every day. articles.title: 5 DIY ideas to create a beautiful mini aquarium at home: simple ways to set up a charming aquatic corner on a budget
articles.summary: There’s something calming about watching water move and tiny plants sway.
articles.body: There’s something calming about watching water move and tiny plants sway. The good news is you don’t need a big tank or a big budget to bring that feeling home. With a few everyday containers and some simple supplies, you can set up a small aquatic corner that looks lovely and takes very little effort to maintain.Glass jar or fishbowl aquariumStart with a large, clean glass jar or an old fishbowl. Add a layer of washed pebbles or sand at the bottom, then a few hardy aquatic plants like java fern or anubias. Fill it with dechlorinated water, and you have a simple, elegant centrepiece for a study table or shelf. It works beautifully as a plant-only setup, or with a single betta fish if the container is large enough and has a lid.Terrarium-style aquascapeUse a clear rectangular container and arrange small rocks, driftwood and moss to create a miniature landscape. Layer the stones with larger ones at the back and smaller ones in front so the scene has depth. It’s like a tiny underwater garden, and every corner looks different from every angle.Recycled container tankOld glass storage jars, clear food containers and even an unused glass vase can be given a second life as mini tanks. Wash them thoroughly, decorate with pebbles and plants, and you’ve got a charming display without spending much. Just make sure the container is food-safe glass and free of cracks.Fairy-light bottle aquariumPlace a string of waterproof LED lights inside or around a large glass bottle or jar. Add shells, smooth stones and a few artificial plants for a dreamy night-time glow. It’s a lovely decorative piece for a bedroom or living room corner, especially in the evening.Shell and pebble beach sceneFill a shallow glass bowl with fine sand, shells and tiny stones to mimic a quiet seaside. Add a few small plants or a miniature figurine for personality. It needs almost no upkeep, and it brings a bit of the beach indoors.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Trump seeks exit, Iran defiant: Key issues holding up peace deal as Qatar brokers talks
articles.summary: A war that neither side appears ready to end on the other's terms is now pushing the United States and Iran back towards the negotiating table.
articles.body: A war that neither side appears ready to end on the other's terms is now pushing the United States and Iran back towards the negotiating table. With Donald Trump facing growing domestic pressure over the conflict and Tehran refusing to surrender its strategic leverage, Qatar has stepped in to broker an agreement.But despite renewed diplomatic efforts, deep divisions over Iran's nuclear programme, sanctions and control of the Strait of Hormuz continue to stand in the way of a breakthrough.According to CNN, the United States and Iran are exploring a diplomatic framework to prevent the conflict from escalating again. Qatar has emerged as the principal mediator, circulating a draft agreement between Washington and Tehran, with both sides making amendments to the proposal.Trump told CNN that renewed US military attacks were highly unlikely if Iran made progress towards an agreement. However, secretary of state Marco Rubio has indicated that negotiations remain difficult, with several Iranian demands considered unacceptable by Washington.The diplomatic push comes amid growing political pressure on Trump following Republican losses in the November 3 midterm elections. The war and its economic consequences, particularly rising energy prices, have become significant political concerns for his administration.Iran has also pushed for an early resumption of negotiations, demanding that Washington lift its naval blockade, remove sanctions and end the war across all fronts.On November 9, Iranian foreign ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei defended Tehran's proposal, describing it as reasonable. However, Washington has expressed reservations over Iran's conditions.What does each side want?The biggest challenge in the negotiations is the gap between Washington's demands and Tehran's conditions. While the US wants to restrict Iran's nuclear capabilities and ensure unrestricted access to the Strait of Hormuz, Iran is seeking economic relief, an end to the blockade and recognition of its strategic interests.Washington wants Iran to agree to restrictions that would prevent it from developing nuclear weapons. A key demand is the dilution or transfer abroad of Iran's stockpile of highly enriched uranium, which remains a major concern for the US.The Trump administration also wants the Strait of Hormuz reopened for unrestricted international shipping, ensuring that Tehran cannot use the strategic waterway as leverage against the US and its regional partners.Tehran, meanwhile, is seeking the removal of US economic sanctions, the release of frozen Iranian assets held abroad and an end to the American naval blockade.Iran also wants recognition of its proposed arrangements for managing the Strait of Hormuz and an end to hostilities across all fronts. Another major demand involves compensation for the killing of Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei and senior Iranian military commanders.Iran has maintained that its nuclear programme is intended for peaceful purposes and that it will not surrender its nuclear rights without receiving meaningful concessions from Washington.What is preventing a deal?Despite renewed diplomatic efforts, major disagreements over Iran's nuclear programme, the Strait of Hormuz and sanctions continue to obstruct an agreement.Washington wants Iran to dilute or transfer its enriched uranium stockpile and guarantee unrestricted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. Tehran, however, is unwilling to give up its nuclear leverage or its influence over the strategic waterway without sanctions relief, the release of frozen assets and an end to the US blockade.A deep trust deficit further complicates negotiations, with Iran wary of another military attack after the conflict began during diplomatic engagement. Trump also faces pressure to end the war without appearing to concede to Tehran, while Iranian hardliners oppose major concessions.Rubio's criticism of Iran's demands as unrealistic further highlights the distance between the two sides, leaving Qatar's mediation facing a difficult path towards a breakthrough.You use AI every day.
