articles.title: 5 foreign policy priorities for Democrats in the next Congress
articles.summary: Democrats charting America’s foreign policy in the next Congress are charged with answering Americans’ demands to bring down soaring prices linked to the war in Iran and President Trump’s tariffs. At the same time, they’re focused on reversing what they view as Trump’s destructive policies: gutting America’s diplomatic corps, slashing foreign assistance and spending federal…
articles.body:
Democrats charting America’s foreign policy in the next Congress are charged with answering Americans’ demands to bring down soaring prices linked to the war in Iran and President Trump’s tariffs.

At the same time, they’re focused on reversing what they view as Trump’s destructive policies: gutting America’s diplomatic corps, slashing foreign assistance and spending federal funds without Congress’s approval.

Democrats are likely to exercise their subpoena power to investigate corruption allegations across the Trump administration and confront other perceived threats to U.S. national security. But some former congressional staff are warning against theatrical hearings that contribute to partisan polarization.

“While oversight and investigations are necessary, I don’t think that the American public wants to see people subpoenaed and called in for things that, obviously, are just for show. I think they want to see actual concrete results,” said Algene Sajery, former Democratic policy director for the Senate Foreign Relations Committee and senior fellow for the National Security Institute.

Here are the top five priorities for Democrats on foreign policy:

Sen. Chris Coons (D-Del.) is viewed as the likely next chair of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, and he has signaled a subpoena is coming for Elon Musk, the tech billionaire, top Republican donor and close ally to Trump.

Musk’s involvement in shutting off his Starlink and Starshield satellite communications in Ukraine in October — an action that left Ukraine defenseless in the face of Russian missile bombardment — was the focus of Coons’s threat.

But Musk also directed the elimination of America’s humanitarian assistance bureau, the U.S. Agency for International Development (USAID), in the first few months of Trump’s term. Democrats want an accounting of the lives lost because of USAID’s shutdown.

Researchers connected the global health cuts to hundreds of thousands of deaths , some two-thirds of which were children. More than 14 million additional deaths are projected to occur around the world by 2030 because of USAID’s shutdown.

The impact on U.S. national security is also not fully understood and ripe for investigation.

“If you want to keep our country secure and prosperous, it’s not through the bombs, you’ve got to do it with the soft power,” said Rep. Lois Frankel (D-Fla.), the likely incoming chair of the House Appropriations Subcommittee on State, Foreign Operations and Related Programs. She was quoting her son, a former USAID employee.

Frankel said another focus will be spotlighting how the administration is spending money outside the directives of Congress. She brought up the example of the administration choosing to destroy millions of dollars’ worth of taxpayer-funded contraception because it contradicted Trump’s policies.

“And I said to Marco Rubio, ‘What’s going on?’ He says to me — this is in public — ‘We’re not in the business of family planning.’ Really? Are you kidding me?” Frankel recounted, referring to Secretary of State Marco Rubio.

“There’s an example of not even doing what we’ve asked them to do, with the money we’ve given them.”

A State Department spokesperson said the agency does not comment on the secretary’s “purported private conversations” with members of Congress.

Democrats have telegraphed they want to withhold funding for Trump’s war against Iran as a way to assert Congress’s authority over the military.

“The Vietnam War ended when Congress finally pulled the plug on paying for it. We should not be providing any funds for this senseless, illegal war in Iran,” Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.) said in an interview last month with “The Federal Effect.”

Van Hollen is a member of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee and Appropriations Committee.

Spending bills provide a vehicle to end funding but could be a yearlong process, said Damian Murphy, senior vice president for national security and international policy at the Center for American Progress. He was the Democratic staff director for the Senate Foreign Relations Committee between 2021 and 2025.

“It’s not a perfect tool, but I do expect that that’s one that many members will be very interested in pursuing,” he said.

The Senate Foreign Relations Committee and House Foreign Affairs Committee will almost surely deploy significant investigative attention to the war.

“The American people deserve answers NOW about our actions in Iran. Why is the Pentagon afraid of the truth?” Coons posted on the social platform X on Oct. 15.

Rep. Gregory Meeks (D-N.Y.), in his bid for chair of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, said he plans to bring resolutions to the floor “immediately” to terminate the war with Iran. It’s an imperfect solution facing a veto from the president and not enough votes in the Senate to override it.

Meeks’s other priorities include protecting the State Department’s nonpartisan foreign and civil service in the face of the Trump administration’s large-scale layoffs, increased use of political appointees and alleged loyalty tests meted out during interviews for senior assignments.

In a brief interview with The Hill last month, Meeks criticized Trump’s “two real estate dealers” driving U.S. foreign policy, referring to the president’s son-in-law Jared Kushner and business partner and close friend Steve Witkoff.

“The State Department, its functionality, or nonfunctioning, is something that the committee has to look at and make some determinations about,” he told The Hill last month.

In a letter to colleagues announcing his bid for the chairmanship, Meeks said he wants to pass a State Department reauthorization bill, which would identify funding priorities, as part of the next Congress. The goal would be to place “guardrails on the Administration’s lawlessness,” protect the diplomatic and career workforce and ensure “our diplomatic capabilities are fully used on behalf of the American people.”

Meeks added the House Foreign Affairs Committee will coordinate with House committees where priorities overlap: the Armed Services, Intelligence and Ways and Means committees.

“We’re talking among ourselves to work collectively together, and respecting each other’s jurisdictions, but also making sure that we are giving our input … working together and … not stepping on one another’s toes,” he said.

Foreign military assistance, Israel, Ukraine

Meeks added that support for Ukraine will be a priority for his chairmanship.

“I will continue to advance a principled foreign policy grounded in our values, including support for Ukraine against Russian aggression,” he wrote in his letter to colleagues.

A more divisive issue for Democrats is military assistance for Israel. A wave of progressive lawmakers will further inflame divisions in the caucus over future U.S.-Israel ties.

Frankel oversees U.S. military assistance to Israel, and the subcommittee’s fiscal 2027 bill — which passed the House in July — includes $3.8 billion in annual funding for the Jewish state.

While Trump announced on Election Day that U.S. funding for Israel would be phased out by the end of the year, the president’s critics and supporters alike pointed to that money being shifted to a controversial joint U.S.-Israeli defense technology cooperation program.

Frankel said she supports the program, which is laid out in Section 219 of the National Defense Authorization Act.

“There’s a lot of, obviously, anti-Israel sentiment, and keeping in mind though, I think this is something that’s not really understood or talked about, the compatibility of the U.S. and Israeli military keeping that region secure,” she said.

Rights groups have come out against Section 219, saying it gives Israel “dangerous” influence over the U.S. defense industry at a time when U.S. interests are “diverging” from Israel and public opinion is increasingly against deeper ties, Reuters reported .

Democrats have tools to counter Trump’s tariffs, many of which were put in place after the Supreme Court dismissed his legal rationale for an earlier tariff regime. The average tariff rate on all imports is currently 9.6 percent, according to the Tax Policy Center .

The Senate Finance Committee is likely the main venue for reining in the president’s tariffs, and the Senate Foreign Relations Committee can use its oversight powers to press for greater accountability, said Sajery, of the National Security Institute.

Sajery said Coons is the type of lawmaker who pushes for concrete results rather than oversight simply for oversight’s sake, with a reputation as a successful bipartisan operator.

“I think he will really appeal to folks who want to find commonsense solutions to mitigate the economic impact of Trump’s failed foreign policies,” she said.

“I think he’ll immediately look at how to restore confidence in the American people that foreign policy is being prosecuted in a way that really takes into consideration their interests, and that economic security is central to the foreign policy agenda.”

articles.title: Trump: ‘A lot of people didn’t like’ Vance comments blaming midterm losses on Iran war
articles.summary: President Trump said “a lot of people didn’t like” Vice President Vance blaming the GOP’s election losses on the Iran war, which has proven to be unpopular across the country. When asked if Vance’s statement following the results of last week’s midterms had impacted their relationship, Trump told reporters, “No, not at all.” “But a…
articles.body:
President Trump said “a lot of people didn’t like” Vice President Vance blaming the GOP’s election losses on the Iran war , which has proven to be unpopular across the country.

When asked if Vance’s statement following the results of last week’s midterms had impacted their relationship, Trump told reporters, “No, not at all.”

“But a lot of people didn’t like his comments. But not me,” he added.

“He was right, other than one thing. He should have made one other statement. One statement that I think is very important. If you had it to do again? Would you do it again? The answer is yes,” the president continued. “I can tell you, if I had it to do again, this historically, for history, will go down as one of the best things we ever did.”

Vance released a lengthy social media post that detailed why he believed the GOP lost in key battleground elections this cycle.

“The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night,” he wrote. “If you’d like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so. Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that’s at least honest.”

The vice president was referring to Trump partially blaming the Middle East conflict for Republicans falling short last week. Vance received pushback from both sides of the aisle for the comment.

The president told The Wall Street Journal late Tuesday that the war with Iran, now in its eighth month, “was a piece of it” in an election night interview.

Asked during an interview on CBS’s “60 Minutes” about Vance’s post and whether he knew it was coming, Trump said: “He asked me, ‘What do I think?’ I said, ‘Write what you feel.’”

He also defended the war effort in the recent interview, saying he believed “historically this will be a very good decision” because “you can’t let Iran have a nuclear weapon.”

“Is it a good decision for today and tomorrow? Maybe not, but you know, I have to go with what’s right for our country,” he added. “If they had a nuclear weapon during my term, I would be excoriated far worse than what happened. I’ve stopped them from having a nuclear weapon. That’s a big thing.”

Trump left the door open to renewing military action against Iran but said it was unlikely if peace talks progressed.

articles.title: Rubio: Iran war not ‘necessarily popular,’ but needed
articles.summary: Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Sunday defended President Trump’s decision to enter the conflict with Iran, arguing that the administration had to confront a national security threat even if doing so was politically unpopular. His backing of the war comes nearly a week after Republicans faced a crushing defeat in the midterm elections and…
articles.body:
Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Sunday defended President Trump’s decision to enter the conflict with Iran, arguing that the administration had to confront a national security threat even if doing so was politically unpopular .

His backing of the war comes nearly a week after Republicans faced a crushing defeat in the midterm elections and lost control of the House and Senate for the next term. Trump and Vice President acknowledged that the war played a role in the party’s nationwide losses.

“The President of the United States identified a very real threat to this country that’s existed for a very long period of time, and he addressed it,” Rubio told reporters at Homestead Air Reserve Base in Florida.

“And he addressed it even though, oftentimes, the right thing to do for the country — confronting difficult challenges for the security of our country — doing it isn’t necessarily popular but necessary,” he added.

Rubio, who has been viewed as a possible top contender for the Republican nomination in the 2028 presidential election, declined to say whether he believed the war was worth the political cost, insisting that his role as secretary of State required him to stay out of domestic politics.

His remarks came ahead of his meeting with his G7 counterparts in Paris on Monday. It marks his first overseas trip since the election, as U.S. allies sought clarity on Trump’s foreign policy agenda following the midterms.

The two-day gathering, which includes foreign ministers from the U.S., United Kingdom, Canada, France, Germany, Italy and Japan, comes as the Trump administration faces pressure to resolve the wars in Iran and Ukraine — with questions surrounding whether Democrats’ takeover of Congress will affect Washington’s approach to the conflicts.

The Iran war, now in its eighth month, became a political liability for the Trump administration that many cited as the reason for the GOP’s poor showing at the polls last week.

“The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night,” Vance wrote in a lengthy post on social media in the aftermath of the election. “If you’d like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so. Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that’s at least honest.”

Trump has also acknowledged that the conflict, which caused rising inflation and gas prices to surge, contributed to Republicans’ losses, but maintained that his decision to strike was necessary to prevent Tehran from developing a nuclear weapon.

articles.title: Even this blue wave probably won’t wash tariffs away
articles.summary: While a Democratic shift in Congress might alter the tone of American trade policy, the underlying bipartisan commitment to economic security and industrial policy suggests that major tariffs and trade restrictions will likely persist.
articles.body:
Nearly two-thirds of Americans blame President Trump for higher prices at the gas pump and in the grocery aisle, citing trade policies and the war with Iran for driving inflation. But the Democratic swing in Congress is unlikely to produce a fundamental reversal of the tariffs and other trade restrictions that have punished U.S. households and strained relations with allies .

Tariffs have never been just a Trump priority . Over the past decade, a bipartisan consensus has formed in opposition to free trade. The debate between Democrats and Republicans became less about whether to protect the U.S. economy and more about how best to protect it.

White House priorities reflected that consensus. It was just a few years ago that the Biden administration was accused of copying Trump’s “America First” approach with its “Build Back Better” program. Those two strategies were not exactly the same . Biden leaned more heavily on industrial policies like grants and subsidies than Trump. But Biden also expanded several of Trump’s tariffs on China, raising Section 301 tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles from 25 percent to 100 percent, increasing duties on certain steel and aluminum products to 25 percent, and raising semiconductor tariffs from 25 percent to 50 percent.

These were not minor adjustments. They showed Democrats’ willingness to expand industrial policy and counter Chinese competition. A return to the pre-Trump consensus on trade would make that political project considerably harder.

Not much has changed for Democrats since then. Despite strong incentives to oppose Trump policies, Democrats still hope to recapture their former working-class base by emphasizing manufacturing jobs and wages.

This middle-ground approach was visible in several of the midterms’ highest-profile campaigns, including those of Democrat James Talarico in Texas and Democrat Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan , who have called for selective tariff reductions, not a return to broad-based free trade.

Being more selective means targeting fewer of the allies and partners on which U.S. markets depend. Following the Supreme Court’s February decision invalidating Trump’s use of emergency powers to impose tariffs , the administration introduced a temporary 10 percent global import surcharge under Section 122 of the Trade Act of 1974 . That measure expired on July 24 and was replaced by new Section 301 duties targeting 60 trading partners over alleged failures to adequately restrict imports produced using forced labor.

The new duties generally impose an additional 10 percent tariff on imports from nearly 20 economies, including Canada, Mexico, Britain and India. The European Union, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan and Switzerland face rates structured to bring combined duties with existing most-favored-nation tariffs to 10 percent or 12.5 percent.

Reducing barriers on key allies makes economic and strategic sense. But China is a different story.

Chinese imports face multiple overlapping measures, including Section 301 tariffs ranging from 7.5 percent to 100 percent , as well as the new 12.5 percent forced-labor-related duty. And the Trump administration’s broader negotiations with Beijing have produced limited tariff relief. Instead, trade restrictions have expanded in the form of controls on advanced technology products and services.

Democrats now find themselves facing three goals: lowering prices at home, rebuilding relationships abroad, and grappling with China. And accomplishing all three goals at once is difficult.

Democrats could seek to reduce some of the most disruptive measures against traditional allies, particularly where tariffs undermine cooperation with Europe, Japan, Canada and South Korea.

But reducing friction with allies is not the same as embracing free trade. A Democratic Congress could just as readily support stronger domestic manufacturing incentives, targeted restrictions on Chinese imports, and expanded investment in semiconductors, batteries, critical minerals, pharmaceuticals and clean-energy technologies. Indeed, the Biden administration demonstrated that industrial policy and protectionist trade measures can operate together.

There are also institutional constraints. Congress has delegated significant trade-policy authority to presidents from both parties. Much of modern tariff policy rests on executive authorities, including Sections 232 and 301 of existing trade legislation . Congress can exercise oversight, change statutory authorities and influence appropriations. However, changing the political balance in the House or Senate does not automatically remove tariffs already imposed through executive action. Nor would a Democratic majority necessarily agree on how far to go in limiting presidential authority, particularly when some of those same powers could be useful to a future Democratic president.

Ultimately, the midterms may alter the tone and priorities of American trade policy more than its underlying direction. There remains a bipartisan consensus that economic security, domestic manufacturing capacity, and technological leadership are the core objectives of American economic policy. The disagreement is about which instruments to use — and which countries to target.

Jeffrey Kucik, Ph.D., is a fellow at the Wahba Initiative for Strategic Competition and an adjunct project of political science and law at the University of Arizona
